items.title: Q1 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.stem: Which British University figures in William Wordsworth's Prelude ?

structured.lead: Which British University figures in William Wordsworth's Prelude ?
structured.options_hint: Durham Glasgow Cambridge Oxford

items.explanation: Book III of William Wordsworth's autobiographical poem The Prelude (1850), titled 'Residence at Cambridge', recounts the poet's undergraduate years at St John's College, University of Cambridge (1787–91).

items.title: Q2 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Middleton
items.stem: Who is the author of A Woman Killed with Kindness ?

structured.lead: Who is the author of A Woman Killed with Kindness ?
structured.options_hint: John Marston Thomas Middleton John Fletc

items.explanation: Thomas Heywood wrote the Elizabethan domestic tragedy A Woman Killed with Kindness (performed 1603, printed 1607), which portrays John Frankford's non-violent punishment of his unfaithful wife Anne.

items.title: Q3 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit I: Drama · William Congreve
items.stem:
In William Congreve's The Way of the World identify the speaker of the line : "One's
cruelty is one's power, and when one parts with one's cruelty, one parts with one's power."

structured.lead: In William Congreve's The Way of the World identify the speaker of the line : "One's cruelty is one's power, and when one parts with one's cruelty, one parts with one's power."
structured.options_hint: Mirabell Witwoud Millamant Mincing

items.explanation: In Act II of William Congreve's Restoration comedy The Way of the World (1700), the witty heroine Millamant speaks this line to Mirabell while defending her right to tease her suitors before surrendering her independence in marriage.

items.title: Q4 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: T.S. Eliot found spiritual support in

structured.lead: T.S. Eliot found spiritual support in
structured.options_hint: Christianity Hinduism Buddhism Judaism

items.explanation: T. S. Eliot formally converted to Anglo-Catholicism (the Church of England) in 1927, declaring himself 'classicist in literature, royalist in politics, and anglo-catholic in religion'. His later works such as Ash-Wednesday (1930) and Four Quartets (1943) are deeply rooted in Christian spirituality.

items.title: Q5 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: By what name is Gulliver known in Brobdingnag ?

structured.lead: By what name is Gulliver known in Brobdingnag ?
structured.options_hint: Grildrig Glumdalclitch Splacknuck Mannik

items.explanation: In Part II of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), the farmer's nine-year-old daughter in Brobdingnag names Gulliver 'Grildrig' (meaning 'manikin' or 'little man'), while Gulliver calls her 'Glumdalclitch' ('little nurse').

items.title: Q6 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who among the following was born in India ?

structured.lead: Who among the following was born in India ?
structured.options_hint: Paul Scott Lawrence Durrell Forster Naip

items.explanation: British novelist and poet Lawrence Durrell (author of The Alexandria Quartet) was born in Jalandhar, British India, on February 27, 1912, to British colonial parents. Paul Scott and E. M. Forster were born in London, while V. S. Naipaul was born in Trinidad.

items.title: Q7 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser
items.stem:
What metaphor does Edmund Spenser employ (Faerie Queene Book 1 Canto 12) to frame
his tale and to describe the relationship between the tale and its readers ?

structured.lead: What metaphor does Edmund Spenser employ (Faerie Queene Book 1 Canto 12) to frame his tale and to describe the relationship between the tale and its readers ?
structured.options_hint: That of a caravan of lost souls, travers

options: That of a caravan of lost souls, traversing a desert
That of a stagecoach, which picks up diverse passengers along the way
That of a ship filled with jolly mariners
That of a riderless horse, following his own direction
items.explanation: At the opening and close of Book I, Canto XII of The Faerie Queene (1590), Edmund Spenser compares his epic poem to a sea voyage in a ship filled with 'jolly Mariners' arriving safely in port to rest before setting sail again.

items.title: Q8 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Who among the following is not associated with Russian formalism ?

structured.lead: Who among the following is not associated with Russian formalism ?
structured.options_hint: Roman Jakobson Georges Poulet Boris Eich

items.explanation: Belgian critic Georges Poulet (1902–1991) was a leading figure of the Geneva School of phenomenological criticism, which viewed reading as an encounter with an author's consciousness. Roman Jakobson, Boris Eichenbaum, and Viktor Shklovsky were all core members of Russian Formalism.

items.title: Q9 · July 2016 (Paper II)

structured.lead: Which character in Dickens keeps on hoping that "something will turn up" ?
structured.options_hint: Barkis Micawber Uriah Heep Miss Havisham

items.explanation: In Charles Dickens's novel David Copperfield (1849–50), the eternally optimistic and debt-ridden Wilkins Micawber—modelled on Dickens's father John Dickens—repeatedly expresses his faith that 'something will turn up'.

items.title: Q10 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Herman Melville

structured.lead: What is the name of the boat that rescues Ishmael in Herman Melville's Moby Dick ?
structured.options_hint: Pequod Rachel Hagar Sphinx

items.explanation: In the Epilogue of Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851), after the white whale sinks the Pequod, the sole survivor Ishmael is rescued from the sea by the cruising whaling ship Rachel, which is searching for its captain's lost sons.

items.title: Q11 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Jane Austen
items.stem: Northanger Abbey is a parody of the _______ romance

structured.lead: Northanger Abbey is a parody of the _______ romance
structured.options_hint: Oriental French Gothic Popular

items.explanation: Jane Austen's novel Northanger Abbey (completed 1803, published posthumously in 1817) is a satirical parody of late eighteenth-century Gothic romances, particularly Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794), which overstimulate the imagination of its young heroine Catherine Morland.

items.title: Q13 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following is another term to describe "art for art's sake" ?

structured.lead: Which of the following is another term to describe "art for art's sake" ?
structured.options_hint: Aestheticism Didacticism Realism Neo-rea

items.explanation: Aestheticism was the late nineteenth-century European arts movement—championed in England by Walter Pater and Oscar Wilde—centred on the doctrine of 'art for art's sake' (l'art pour l'art), which held that art should pursue beauty rather than moral or didactic purposes.

items.title: Q14 · July 2016 (Paper II)

structured.lead: The statement that there are "none so credulous as infidels" is an illustration of
structured.options_hint: Oxymoron Antithesis Paradox Metonomy

items.explanation: The statement 'there are none so credulous as infidels' (asserting that unbelievers are the most gullible believers) is a paradox—a seemingly self-contradictory statement that upon reflection reveals an unexpected truth.

items.title: Q18 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In King Lear for what reason does Kent assume a disguise ?

structured.lead: In King Lear for what reason does Kent assume a disguise ?
structured.options_hint: To continue to serve Lear, though Lear h

options: To continue to serve Lear, though Lear has banished him
To revenge upon Lear for banishing him
items.explanation: In Act I, Scene 4 of William Shakespeare's King Lear, the loyal Earl of Kent—banished for defending Cordelia—returns in disguise as the plain-spoken servant Caius so that he can continue to serve and protect Lear faithfully.

items.title: Q19 · July 2016 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: What is a feminine rhyme ?

structured.lead: What is a feminine rhyme ?
structured.options_hint: A rhyme on two syllables in which the la

options: A rhyme on two syllables in which the last syllable is unstressed
A poem in which every third syllable rhymes
items.explanation: A feminine rhyme (or double rhyme) is a rhyme that matches two syllables in which the first syllable is stressed and the final syllable is unstressed (such as 'pleasure/treasure' or 'motion/ocean').

items.explanation: At the very beginning of 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1919), T. S. items.stem: Who of the following is a Cavalier poet ?

structured.lead: Who of the following is a Cavalier poet ?
structured.options_hint: George Herbert John Donne Robert Herrick

items.explanation: Robert Herrick (1591–1674), author of Hesperides (1648) and 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time', was a leading Cavalier poet and one of the 'Sons of Ben' (followers of Ben Jonson). John Donne, George Herbert, and Andrew Marvell are classified as Metaphysical poets.

items.explanation: The Transcendence of the Ego (La Transcendance de l'Ego, 1936) is an early existentialist-phenomenological essay by Jean-Paul Sartre, whereas Of Grammatology (1967), Of Spirit: Heidegger and the Question (1987), and The Work of Mourning (2001) are works by Jacques Derrida.

items.explanation: In Book I of John Milton's Paradise Lost (line 692, referring to Mammon's mining of gold in Hell), the phrase 'precious bane' ('valuable poison/curse') combines two contradictory terms into a compact phrase and is an example of an oxymoron.

Shakespeare to observe most successfully ?
structured.options_hint: Time Place Action Johnson does not feel

items.explanation: In his Preface to Shakespeare (1765), Samuel Johnson argues that the unities of time and place are unnecessary illusions, whereas Shakespeare 'has well enough preserved the unity of action', since his plots follow a coherent causal progression from beginning through middle to end.

items.title: Q37 · July 2016 (Paper II)

structured.lead: Which of the following statements does not describe Michel Foucault's position ?
structured.options_hint: Foucault's work sexuality is literally w

options: Foucault's work sexuality is literally written on the body
There is connection between power and knowledge
Where there is power, it is possible to find resistance
items.explanation: In The History of Sexuality (1976), Michel Foucault argues that power operates through discourse, that power and knowledge are mutually constitutive, and that 'where there is power, there is resistance'. He rejects the notion that sexuality is a literal or natural inscription on the body prior to discourse.

structured.options_hint: Far from the madding crowd A youth to Fo

options: A youth to Fortune and Fame unknown
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen
All nature is but art, unknown to thee
items.explanation: The line 'All nature is but art, unknown to thee' is from Epistle I of Alexander Pope's An Essay on Man (1733–34). The other three famous phrases—'Far from the madding crowd', 'A youth to Fortune and to Fame unknown', and 'Full many a flower is born to blush unseen'—all originate in Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' (1751).

items.explanation: Robert Browning's dramatic monologue 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' (published in Dramatis Personae, 1864) is a spirited defence of old age against youth, famously opening with the lines: 'Grow old along with me! / The best is yet to be, / The last of life, for which the first was made.'

structured.lead: In Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, the pilgrims, like the medieval society of which they are a part, are made up of three social groups or "estates". What are the three estates ?
structured.options_hint: Nobility, church and commoners Royalty,

items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer's General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales organizes its portrait of medieval English society around the traditional three estates: the nobility/military (those who fight, like the Knight), the church/clergy (those who pray), and the commoners/laity (those who work).

items.stem: When was the English ban on James Joyce's Ulysses lifted ?

structured.lead: When was the English ban on James Joyce's Ulysses lifted ?

items.explanation: Following Judge John M. Woolsey's landmark 1933 US ruling, the British ban on James Joyce's Ulysses (1922) was lifted in 1936 when The Bodley Head published the first legal English edition in London.

items.title: Q48 · July 2016 (Paper II)

items.stem: Who among the following is not an imagist ?

structured.lead: Who among the following is not an imagist ?
structured.options_hint: Ezra Pound Yeats Amy Lowell Hulme

items.explanation: W. B. Yeats was an Irish Symbolist and Modernist poet, not an Imagist. T. E. Hulme laid the theoretical foundations of Imagism, Ezra Pound launched the movement in 1912 and edited Des Imagistes (1914), and Amy Lowell led its later phase ('Amygism').
